ground_truth: [M-1] Missing compromise check allows malicious operations The `verifiedProfileIdForAddress` function does not check if an address has been marked as compromised. This allows an attacker with a stolen private key to continue executing unauthorized actions even after the user has flagged the address as compromised.  [M-2] Restored addresses remain marked as compromised When an address is restored after being marked as compromised, the `isAddressCompromised` flag is not reset to `false`. This prevents the restored address from performing any actions on behalf of the profile, defeating the purpose of the restoration feature.
Findings:
Main security & correctness problems

1. Upgradeability / storage‐layout
   • UUPS contract has no “__gap” reserved storage; any future version that adds state will overwrite existing variables (storage-collision risk).  
   • Constructor does not call _disableInitializers(); the implementation itself can be initialised and an attacker could become “owner” of the logic contract and approve malicious upgrades for every proxy that delegates to it.  
   • _authorizeUpgrade() does not enforce onlyProxy / onlyDelegatedCall; the function can be executed directly on the proxy OR on the implementation, making the previous point exploitable.

2. State-inconsistency when deleting an address  
   _deleteAddressAtIndexFromArray() pushes the last element of the array – not the element that is actually being removed – to removedAddresses.  
   The real “deleted” address is silently lost and profileIdByAddress is **not** cleared, so the mapping keeps pointing to a profile that no longer contains the address.  
   This breaks the invariant “every address in profileIdByAddress must be inside profiles[profileId].addresses”, enables phantom memberships and can be abused in logic that relies on that invariant.

3. Denial-of-Service by unbounded loops  
   • bulkInviteAddresses(), addInvitesBatch() and various view helpers iterate over user-supplied arrays with no upper bound → transaction can easily run out of gas and lock critical admin functions (DoS).  
   • _sumInvites(), checkMaxAddresses() and many view functions iterate over growing arrays that can become too large to fit in the block gas limit, permanently freezing those functions (permanent DoS).

4. Missing Reentrancy protection  
   Functions like registerAddress(), uninviteUser(), createProfile() and inviteAddress() change internal state before performing external calls (validateAndSaveSignature(), contractAddressManager lookup).  
   They are non-payable but can still be called by malicious contracts; lack of nonReentrant guard allows re-entering and corrupting mappings / counters.

5. Weak address-compromise logic  
   A profile owner can arbitrarily mark any address inside the profile as “compromised”, preventing that address from being used elsewhere; there is no confirmation from the address owner, enabling griefing.

6. Incorrect invite removal bookkeeping  
   In _inviterProfileAuthorizedSender() and uninviteUser() the mapping sentInviteIndexByProfileIdAndAddress is updated for the moved element but acceptedIdIndexByProfileIdAndId is never updated, leaving stale indices that can later cause AddressNotInvited / out-of-bounds errors.

7. Insufficient validation in incrementProfileCount()  
   Any caller that controls ETHOS_REVIEW or ETHOS_ATTESTATION address in ContractAddressManager can mint unlimited “mock” profiles, bypassing the whole invite tree and exhausting storage.

8. Time-of-check / time-of-use (TOCTOU) on compromised flag  
   deleteAddressAtIndex() sets isAddressCompromised before the address is removed; if the call re-enters, the same address is already considered compromised but still present in the array, breaking later assumptions.

9. Miscellaneous
   • getProfile() silently allows id == profileCount-1 even if the profile is a “mock” (profile.profileId == 0) ⇒ returns an empty struct without reverting.  
   • registerAddress() allows anyone (not necessarily the address owner) to associate addresses with a profile as long as they possess a signature; replay protection relies only on address/profile/randValue hashing – no domain separator – permitting cross-contract replay attacks.  
   • Several public mappings (e.g. sentAt) leak timestamps that may be considered private / deanonymising.  
   • Events emitted after state change although revert can still happen later in the same transaction through re-entrancy (mainly for registerAddress).

These issues combine to open the door for storage corruption, denial-of-service, privilege escalation during upgrades and invite / membership forgery.

**Report Description**:

This prevents the restored address from performing any actions on behalf of the profile, effectively defeating the purpose of the restoration feature. This issue can lead to a denial of service for restored addresses.

ground_truth: [M-3] Corruptible Upgradability Pattern The UUPS upgradeability pattern is implemented incorrectly. Inherited contracts are missing storage gaps, non-upgradeable base contracts are used instead of their upgrade-safe alternatives, and initializers are not disabled in constructors. These flaws could lead to storage corruption during a contract upgrade.
Findings:
Main issues in SignatureControl.sol

1. Signature-malleability bypass  
   • Only the raw bytes of the signature are stored as “used”.  
   • If the verifier accepts both (v = 27 / 28 or high-s / low-s) variants, an attacker can reuse an already-executed message with a different but still valid (r,s,v) combination and pass the onlyUnusedSignature check (re-entrance / replay).

2. Replay / cross-domain risk  
   • messageHash is supplied by the caller and the contract does not insist on a domain separator, chain-id, contract-address, function selector, nonce, etc.  
   • Even if the same hash were rejected, the attacker can sign the identical business payload on another chain or for another contract and reuse it here.

3. Missing storage gap for upgradeable contracts  
   • The contract inherits from Initializable but does not reserve the usual 50-slot __gap.  
   • On future upgrades new variables may overwrite mapping data or critical state.

4. Gas-griefing vector via unbounded “bytes” keys  
   • signatureUsed mapping accepts arbitrary-length bytes.  
   • A malicious implementation of validateAndSaveSignature (in a derived contract) could be DoSed with extremely long signatures that consume excessive gas when copied / hashed.

5. Trust-assumption on signatureVerifier  
   • expectedSigner / signatureVerifier can be changed by any internal call.  
   • If a child contract exposes those internal setters without proper access control, anyone can redirect verification to a back-doored verifier or change the signer to themselves. The base contract offers no protection.

6. No zero-address check at construction time for the contract itself  
   • Failing to initialise (or re-initialise) the contract leaves expectedSigner or signatureVerifier at address(0), making every call revert and bricking any inheriting contract.

These weaknesses together mean signatures can be replayed, state can be corrupted in upgrades, and—depending on how the abstract contract is used—critical parameters might be hijacked or the contract DoSed.

**Report Description**:  
The UUPS (Universal Upgradeable Proxy Standard) upgradeability pattern is implemented incorrectly. The identified issues include:

2. Use of non-upgradeable base contracts instead of their upgrade-safe alternatives, which compromises the integrity of the upgrade process.  
3. Initializers are not disabled in constructors, which can allow re-initialization and lead to unexpected behavior or vulnerabilities.  

These flaws collectively pose a significant risk of storage corruption and functional failure during contract upgrades.

ground_truth: [M-3] Corruptible Upgradability Pattern The UUPS upgradeability pattern is implemented incorrectly. Inherited contracts are missing storage gaps, non-upgradeable base contracts are used instead of their upgrade-safe alternatives, and initializers are not disabled in constructors. These flaws could lead to storage corruption during a contract upgrade.
Findings:
Possible security / reliability issues in the contract

1. Up-gradability foot-gun – no once-only guard  
   • __accessControl_init() is not protected with an {initializer} modifier (onlyInitializing is not enough outside the constructor context).  
   • If the proxy is ever re-initialised through a new implementation that again calls __accessControl_init, all roles and the address-manager can be overwritten.

2. Owner can brick the contract  
   • updateOwner(address(0)) is allowed.  
   • Once the only owner has been revoked and replaced by the zero address, every function protected with onlyOwner becomes permanently inaccessible.

3. Admin can brick, or capture, the pause mechanism  
   • updateContractAddressManager(address(0)) makes onlyInteractionControl permanently revert → pause / unpause can never be executed again.  
   • An admin can point contractAddressManager to a malicious contract that returns an arbitrary address for ETHOS_INTERACTION_CONTROL, allowing the admin to pause / unpause at will (RBAC bypass).

4. Missing zero-address checks in several functions  
   • addAdmin(), updateContractAddressManager(), updateExpectedSigner(), updateSignatureVerifier() accept address(0) and may disable parts of the system.

5. Fragile use of AccessControlEnumerable  
   • updateOwner() always revokes getRoleMember(OWNER_ROLE, 0).  
   • If more than one OWNER_ROLE holder ever exists (possible through the public grantRole interface), the function can revoke the wrong owner, leaving a malicious owner in place.

6. Potential permanent loss of owner through renounceRole  
   • Because DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE has no members, if the sole owner calls renounceRole(), no one can ever restore OWNER_ROLE or ADMIN_ROLE, locking all privileged functions.

7. No events for critical changes  
   • updateContractAddressManager(), updateExpectedSigner(), updateSignatureVerifier(), pause() and unpause() emit no contract-specific events, hampering monitoring and incident response.

8. Typo in parameter name  
   • updateSignatureVerifier(address sinatureVerifier) – misspelled variable is only cosmetic, but suggests insufficient review.

9. Revert message mismatch  
   • onlyInteractionControl reverts with keccak256("ETHOS_INTERACTION_CONTROL") instead of the constant’s value; if the constant ever changes, the message will be misleading.

Although none of the above is an immediate re-entrancy or arithmetic bug, together they allow role-based privilege escalation or permanent denial-of-service and therefore represent serious vulnerabilities.
